[LLM] CVE-2026-3300 Everest Forms Pro eval() payload in HTTP request to Complex Calculation form Exploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests that carry the literal exploit signature of the Everest Forms Pro Complex Calculation eval() injection: a form-field value starting with a single quote followed by wp_insert_user() and a // PHP comment marker, often with the rogue username 'diksimarina'. Targets the unauthenticated RCE on Everest Forms Pro <=1.9.12 directly at the WAF/web-log layer. Rationale: Uses three article-specific strings: the literal username 'diksimarina' (confirmed by Wordfence and corroborated by The Hacker News and Infosecurity Magazine), the wp_insert_user() PHP function from the injected payload, and the Everest Forms calculation endpoint path. These three tokens combined make HTTP body/query matches very high fidelity. Cross-checked against Wordfence advisory and GHSA-jfqc-5rvh-wp99. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wordfence.com/blog/2026/06/attackers-actively-exploiting-critical-vulnerability-in-everest-forms-pro-plugin/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hackers-exploit-critical-everest-forms.html • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jfqc-5rvh-wp99
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004

   or RemoteUrl has_any ("everest-forms","everest_forms_calculation")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc

title: Everest Forms Pro CVE-2026-3300 eval() Injection Payload in HTTP Request
id: 8f3d2c1b-7a45-4e6d-b1c2-2026330001ee
description: Detects HTTP requests to WordPress sites containing the CVE-2026-3300 Everest Forms Pro Complex Calculation eval() injection signature (wp_insert_user, diksimarina, or single-quote PHP escape against the form endpoint).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-everest-forms-pro-flaw-exploited-to-take-over-wordpress-sites/
  - https://www.wordfence.com/blog/2026/06/attackers-actively-exploiting-critical-vulnerability-in-everest-forms-pro-plugin/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/06
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.004
  - cve.2026.3300
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_method:
    cs-method: 'POST'
  selection_payload:
    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - 'wp_insert_user'
      - 'diksimarina'
      - 'everest_forms_calculation'
  condition: selection_method and selection_payload
falsepositives:
  - Penetration tests or vulnerability scanners targeting the same endpoint
level: high
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:iis OR source:cloudfront OR source:cloudflare) @http.method:POST (@http.url:(*everest-forms* OR *admin-ajax.php*) AND (@http.url:(*wp_insert_user* OR *diksimarina* OR *everest_forms_calculation*) OR @http.url_details.queryString:(*wp_insert_user* OR *diksimarina*) OR @http.useragent:(*sqlmap* OR *python-requests*)))
# log group: /aws/wafv2 or CloudFront real-time logs
fields @timestamp, httpRequest.clientIp, httpRequest.country, httpRequest.uri, httpRequest.args, action, httpRequest.headers.0.value as ua
| filter httpRequest.uri like /everest-forms/ or httpRequest.uri like /admin-ajax/ or httpRequest.args like /wp_insert_user/ or httpRequest.args like /diksimarina/
| filter not isPresent(terminatingRuleId) or action = "ALLOW"
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 200

[LLM] Inbound traffic from CVE-2026-3300 mass-exploitation source IPs to web servers Delivery High
Alerts on any network connection or web request originating from the four IPs Wordfence attributes to the active CVE-2026-3300 exploitation campaign (202.56.2.126, 209.146.60.26, 15.235.166.18, 185.78.165.153). These IPs have driven 29,300+ exploit attempts since 2026-04-13; any successful TCP/HTTP session from them to an internal WordPress host warrants triage. Rationale: Four IPs are explicitly attributed by Wordfence as the primary CVE-2026-3300 exploitation sources (Wordfence flagged 202.56.2.126 and 209.146.60.26 as 'primary' originators). Two additional IPs come from the pre-extracted IOC bundle. Detection is high-fidelity because these IPs are attacker-owned infra with no legitimate business reason to reach internal web servers. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wordfence.com/blog/2026/06/attackers-actively-exploiting-critical-vulnerability-in-everest-forms-pro-plugin/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-everest-forms-pro-flaw-exploited-to-take-over-wordpress-sites/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (ExploitIPs)
| where LocalPort in (80,443,8080,8443) or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","httpd","nginx","apache2","php-fpm","php-cgi.exe")
| summarize ConnectionCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Ports=make_set(LocalPort) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName
| extend Campaign="CVE-2026-3300"
| order by LastSeen desc
let ExploitIPs = dynamic(["202.56.2.126","209.146.60.26","15.235.166.18","185.78.165.153"]);
union isfuzzy=true

   | where SourceIP in (ExploitIPs)
   | project TimeGenerated, src=SourceIP, dest=DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct),
  (W3CIISLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where cIP in (ExploitIPs)

| order by LastSeen desc

[LLM] WordPress 'diksimarina' rogue administrator account activity in web/access logs Installation High
Hunts any HTTP request, log line, or audit entry that references the literal username 'diksimarina' — the rogue WordPress administrator account created by the CVE-2026-3300 wp_insert_user() payload. Per the Wordfence advisory the account also uses the email diksimarina@gmail.com. Catches both the creation request and any subsequent attacker login or wp-admin activity tied to the account. Rationale: The username 'diksimarina' is the single most distinctive IOC in the article — the BleepingComputer body explicitly says administrators should 'review log files and administrator accounts for any suspicious activity, especially containing the string diksimarina.' Wordfence corroborates and adds the email diksimarina@gmail.com. Any production log mention of this string is a strong indicator of a successful CVE-2026-3300 exploit on that host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wordfence.com/blog/2026/06/attackers-actively-exploiting-critical-vulnerability-in-everest-forms-pro-plugin/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hackers-exploit-critical-everest-forms.html • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/everest-forms-pro-rce-actively/
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1078.001 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where RemoteUrl has "diksimarina" or RemoteUrl has "diksimarina%40gmail.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, LocalPort, ActionType
| union (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where FileName has "diksimarina" or FolderPath has "diksimarina" or AdditionalFields has "diksimarina"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 60d;
union isfuzzy=true
  (W3CIISLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
   | where csUriStem has "diksimarina" or csUriQuery has "diksimarina" or csReferer has "diksimarina" or csUserName =~ "diksimarina"
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, src=cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserName, scStatus, csUserAgent),
  (AppServiceHTTPLogs
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
   | where CsUriStem has "diksimarina" or CsUriQuery has "diksimarina" or Referer has "diksimarina"
   | project TimeGenerated, src=CIp, CsMethod, CsUriStem, CsUriQuery, ScStatus, UserAgent),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
   | where RequestURL has "diksimarina" or Message has "diksimarina" or SourceUserName =~ "diksimarina" or DestinationHostName =~ "diksimarina"
   | project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, src=SourceIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, Message),
  (Syslog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
   | where SyslogMessage has "diksimarina"
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SyslogMessage)
| extend ioc="diksimarina", cve="CVE-2026-3300"
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] PHP webshell drop in WordPress wp-content directories by web-server process Installation Medium
Hunts file writes of .php files into wp-content/uploads, wp-content/themes, or wp-content/plugins by IIS/Apache/Nginx/php-fpm worker processes. This is the canonical post-exploitation behaviour the article warns about following diksimarina admin compromise: the attacker uploads webshells or backdoors via the WordPress plugin/theme uploader once admin access is established. Rationale: Article explicitly lists 'planting backdoors and webshells' as the post-compromise impact and notes wp-content/uploads as the typical drop directory implied by 'modifying content, installing plugins and themes'. Pivot is articulated through three high-fidelity constraints: web-server-process parent (w3wp/php-fpm/httpd), WordPress plugin/theme/upload path, and PHP-executable extension — combined this is rarely benign outside of admin-driven plugin installs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wordfence.com/blog/2026/06/attackers-actively-exploiting-critical-vulnerability-in-everest-forms-pro-plugin/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-everest-forms-pro-flaw-exploited-to-take-over-wordpress-sites/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\wp-content\\uploads\\","/wp-content/uploads/","\\wp-content\\plugins\\","/wp-content/plugins/","\\wp-content\\themes\\","/wp-content/themes/")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".phar" or FileName endswith ".php7"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","httpd","nginx","apache2")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RequestSourceIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType =~ "FileCreated" or DvcAction =~ "created"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/wp-content/uploads/","\\wp-content\\uploads\\","/wp-content/plugins/","\\wp-content\\plugins\\","/wp-content/themes/","\\wp-content\\themes\\")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("php","phtml","phar","php7","phps")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","httpd","nginx","apache2")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| extend cve="CVE-2026-3300", note="webshell_drop_candidate"
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      - '\wp-content\uploads\'
      - '/wp-content/plugins/'
      - '\wp-content\plugins\'

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-3300")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Miasma Worm Hits Microsoft Again: Azure Functions Action and 72 Other Repositories Disabled After Supply Chain Attack Targeting AI Coding Agents

StepSecurity
2026-06-06 12 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On June 5, 2026, the Miasma worm campaign reached Microsoft's Azure GitHub organizations. GitHub disabled 73 repositories across four Microsoft GitHub organizations after a malicious commit was pushed to the Azure/durabletask repository using a previously compromised contributor account. The attack planted configuration files that execute a credential-harvesting payload when a developer opens the repository in Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or VS Code.

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious AI coding-agent hook configs written to repo (.claude/.gemini/.cursor/.vscode)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound DNS / HTTP to Miasma C2 (git-service.com / m-kosche.com) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] Malicious AI coding-agent hook configs written to repo (.claude/.gemini/.cursor/.vscode) Installation High
Hunts the Miasma worm's signature artifact: simultaneous creation of SessionStart hooks and folderOpen tasks in .claude/settings.json, .gemini/settings.json, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, and .vscode/tasks.json — all pointing at node .github/setup.js. This is the precise file-set planted in the June 5 2026 Azure/durabletask commit 5f456b8. Rationale: The five planted-file paths are verbatim from the article's 'Five Planted Files, Four Attack Vectors' section. Requiring >=2 co-occurrence per host suppresses single legitimate .vscode/tasks.json edits while keeping near-zero FP on the Miasma file-set. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/ • https://github.com/step-security/supply-chain-firewall
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.claude\settings.json", @"\.gemini\settings.json", @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", @"\.vscode\tasks.json", @"\.github\setup.js")
| extend Artifact = case(
    FolderPath has @"\.claude\settings.json", "claude-hook",
    FolderPath has @"\.gemini\settings.json", "gemini-hook",
    FolderPath has @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", "cursor-prompt-injection",
    FolderPath has @"\.vscode\tasks.json", "vscode-folderopen",
    FolderPath has @"\.github\setup.js", "miasma-payload", "other")
| summarize ArtifactsSeen = make_set(Artifact), Paths = make_set(FolderPath), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where array_length(ArtifactsSeen) >= 2  // co-occurrence of >=2 of the 5 planted files
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.claude\settings.json", @"\.gemini\settings.json", @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", @"\.vscode\tasks.json", @"\.github\setup.js")
| extend Artifact = case(
    TargetFilePath has @"\.claude\settings.json", "claude-hook",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.gemini\settings.json", "gemini-hook",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", "cursor-prompt-injection",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.vscode\tasks.json", "vscode-folderopen",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.github\setup.js", "miasma-payload", "other")
| summarize ArtifactsSeen = make_set(Artifact), Paths = make_set(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| where array_length(ArtifactsSeen) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc

  - attack.t1546

[LLM] node.exe spawned by Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini executing .github/setup.js Exploitation High
Hunts the Miasma worm's automatic execution chain: VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, or Gemini CLI launching node.exe with .github/setup.js as the script argument. This is the runtime detonation produced when a developer simply opens a repo containing the planted hook configs. Rationale: Article quotes the exact command 'node .github/setup.js' invoked by all four planted configs (Claude SessionStart, Gemini SessionStart, Cursor prompt injection, VS Code folderOpen task). Anchoring on parent IDE + node.exe + setup.js path is high-fidelity because legitimate projects rarely store bootstrap scripts under .github/. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/ • https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/tasks#_run-behavior
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@".github\setup.js", ".github/setup.js")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","claude.exe","claude-code.exe","gemini.exe","node.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "node.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@".github\setup.js", ".github/setup.js")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","claude.exe","claude-code.exe","gemini.exe","node.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Outbound DNS / HTTP to Miasma C2 (git-service.com / m-kosche.com) Command & Control High
Hunts resolution or connection to the Miasma worm's credential-exfiltration infrastructure: check.git-service.com, git-service.com, and t.m-kosche.com. These domains receive harvested AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes/dev-tool secrets from the planted payload. Rationale: Three domains are explicitly listed in the article's pre-extracted IOCs (check.git-service.com, t.m-kosche.com, git-service.com). Article says credential-harvesting payload exfiltrates AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes/dev-tool secrets, so DNS+network egress to these domains is high-fidelity C2. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-worm-hits-microsoft-again-azure-functions-action-and-72-other-repositories-disabled-after-supply-chain-attack-targeting-ai-coding-agents

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort

[LLM] Suspicious commit pattern: '[skip ci]' with backdated timestamp adding only IDE config files Delivery Medium
Hunts the Miasma commit fingerprint: a single push where 5 files added / 0 source files modified, commit message ends with '[skip ci]', author date backdated to a pre-2024 timestamp, and the added paths include AI-agent config dirs. Detects via GitHub Audit Log shipped to Sentinel/Defender via CloudAppEvents or to Datadog via the GitHub integration. Rationale: Article details the exact commit fingerprint: commit 5f456b8 with message 'Switched DataConverter to OrchestrationContext [skip ci]', 5 files added / 0 source files modified, backdated to 2020-03-09T15:59:47Z (six years before push). The conjunction of [skip ci] + backdated author date + added IDE-config paths is the Miasma operator signature. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/admin/monitoring-activity-in-your-enterprise/reviewing-audit-logs-for-your-enterprise
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "GitHub"
| where ActionType in ("Repositories.Push","RepositoriesPush","git.push")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has "[skip ci]"
| where Raw has_any (".claude/settings.json",".gemini/settings.json",".cursor/rules/setup.mdc",".vscode/tasks.json",".github/setup.js")
| extend AuthorDate = extract(@"author[^\d]+(\d{4})-\d{2}-\d{2}", 1, Raw)
| where isnotempty(AuthorDate) and toint(AuthorDate) < 2024
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ObjectName, AuthorDate, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
// Requires GitHub Audit Log connector (GitHubAuditLogPolling_CL) or CommonSecurityLog ingest
GitHubAuditLogPolling_CL
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where action_s == "git.push" or action_s == "repo.push"
| where commits_s has "[skip ci]"
| where commits_s has_any (".claude/settings.json",".gemini/settings.json",".cursor/rules/setup.mdc",".vscode/tasks.json",".github/setup.js")
| extend AuthorYear = extract(@"author[^\d]+(\d{4})-\d{2}-\d{2}", 1, commits_s)
| where isnotempty(AuthorYear) and toint(AuthorYear) < 2024
| project TimeGenerated, actor_s, actor_ip_s, repo_s, commits_s, AuthorYear
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:github @evt.name:git.push @commits.message:*"[skip ci]"* (@commits.added:(*.claude/settings.json* OR *.gemini/settings.json* OR *.cursor/rules/setup.mdc* OR *.vscode/tasks.json* OR *.github/setup.js*))
CLOUD
`github_audit` action=git.push | spath input=raw_event | search commits{}.message="*[skip ci]*" (commits{}.added{}="*.claude/settings.json" OR commits{}.added{}="*.gemini/settings.json" OR commits{}.added{}="*.cursor/rules/setup.mdc" OR commits{}.added{}="*.vscode/tasks.json" OR commits{}.added{}="*.github/setup.js") | eval author_year=substr('commits{}.timestamp',1,4) | where author_year<"2024" | table _time repo actor commits{}.id commits{}.message commits{}.added{} author_year
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")

High

Microsoft's durabletask PyPI Package Compromised in Supply Chain Attack

StepSecurity
2026-06-06 14 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Three malicious versions of Microsoft's official durabletask Python SDK were published to PyPI on May 19, 2026. The compromised package silently downloads and executes a 28 KB payload that steals credentials from AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, password managers, and over 90 developer tool configurations, then spreads laterally through cloud infrastructure. The payload skips systems with a Russian locale, a hallmark of Eastern European cybercrime operations. The attack has been linked to the TeamPCP threat group behind the Mini Shai-Hulud campaign.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Pip install of compromised Microsoft durabletask versions 1.4.1-1.4.3
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Microsoft's durabletask PyPI Package Compromised in Supply Chain Attack
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] rope.pyz dropper executed as /tmp/managed.pyz from durabletask import · [LLM] Fake pgsql-monitor.service systemd persistence written under ~/.config/systemd/user/ · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Egress to TeamPCP rope.pyz C2 infrastructure (check.git-service.com / t.m-kosche.com / 160.119.64.3) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] gh auth token / gpg-decrypt credential harvesting by python3 child · [LLM] Burst of AWS SSM SendCommand / StartSession from stolen durabletask credentials · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] Pip install of compromised Microsoft durabletask versions 1.4.1-1.4.3 Delivery High
Hunts for pip / python invocations that explicitly request or have resolved to the three trojanized durabletask versions published to PyPI on 19 May 2026. Targets Linux CI runners, build agents, and cloud workloads where the package would be picked up. Rationale: Anchored on the three article-confirmed malicious versions (1.4.1, 1.4.2, 1.4.3) and the publication window of 19 May 2026 16:19 UTC onward. Process telemetry of explicit `pip install durabletask==X.Y.Z` invocations is high-fidelity since the legitimate prior version is 1.4.0 (Apr 8). Tier=alerting because of specific version pins. No external sources cross-checked.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "durabletask"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "install"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip","pip3","python","python3") or FileName in~ ("pip","pip3","python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("durabletask==1.4.1","durabletask==1.4.2","durabletask==1.4.3")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "durabletask" and ProcessCommandLine !has "durabletask==1.4.0" and ProcessCommandLine !has "durabletask<1.4.1" and Timestamp between (datetime(2026-05-19) .. datetime(2026-05-20T12:00:00Z)))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip","pip3","python","python3")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "durabletask" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "install"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("durabletask==1.4.1","durabletask==1.4.2","durabletask==1.4.3")
   or (ActingProcessCommandLine !has "durabletask==1.4.0" and TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-05-19) .. datetime(2026-05-20T12:00:00Z)))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Compromised Microsoft durabletask PyPI Versions Installed (TeamPCP)
id: 2f4b8d10-9a52-4d3f-9b21-1e7c6a4f2c11
description: Detects pip installation of the trojanized durabletask versions 1.4.1, 1.4.2, or 1.4.3 published by TeamPCP / Mini Shai-Hulud on 19 May 2026.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/microsofts-durabletask-pypi-package-compromised-in-supply-chain-attack
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/05
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1078
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_tool:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/pip'
      - '/pip3'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'durabletask==1.4.1'
      - 'durabletask==1.4.2'
      - 'durabletask==1.4.3'
  condition: selection_tool and selection_cmd
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:(*durabletask==1.4.1* OR *durabletask==1.4.2* OR *durabletask==1.4.3*)) AND @process.command_line:*install*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/(pip3?|python3?(\.\d+)?)$/i
| regex("durabletask==1\\.4\\.[123]", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

[LLM] rope.pyz dropper executed as /tmp/managed.pyz from durabletask import Installation High
Hunts the unique payload-execution fingerprint from the TeamPCP supply chain attack: a python3 process whose command line references /tmp/managed.pyz, typically spawned via start_new_session=True from a parent python3 -c "import durabletask". Highest-fidelity single signal in the campaign. Rationale: /tmp/managed.pyz is the article-confirmed payload filename the dropper writes via urllib.request.urlretrieve and immediately executes with subprocess.Popen(["python3", "/tmp/managed.pyz"]). The string is unique to this campaign — virtually zero benign use of that exact path. Parent-process pivot on `python3 -c "import durabletask"` adds the chain-of-custody. No external sources cross-checked.

[LLM] gh auth token / gpg-decrypt credential harvesting by python3 child Actions on Objectives High
Detects the rope.pyz collector pattern of harvesting GitHub Personal Access Tokens via gh CLI and GPG-protected secrets via `gpg --batch --passphrase anon --decrypt`, parented by a python3 process — exactly the cmdline strings the article ties to managed.pyz parallel collectors. Rationale: Article-verbatim cmdline strings: `gh auth token`, `gh auth status --show-token`, and `gpg --batch --passphrase anon --decrypt`. The literal passphrase `anon` is an attacker-chosen string with no legitimate use — humans do not use that passphrase for real GPG-protected material. Parented by python3 narrows out interactive developer use of gh. No external sources cross-checked.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.005 T1555 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3")
| where (FileName =~ "gh" and (ProcessCommandLine has "auth token" or ProcessCommandLine has "auth status --show-token"))
   or (FileName =~ "gpg" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("--batch","--passphrase anon","--decrypt"))
| summarize CommandCount = count(),
            Commands = make_set(ProcessCommandLine),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
         by DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where CommandCount >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName in~ ("python","python3")
| where (ActingProcessName =~ "gh" and (ActingProcessCommandLine has "auth token" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "auth status --show-token"))
   or (ActingProcessName =~ "gpg" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("--batch","--passphrase anon","--decrypt"))
| summarize CommandCount = count(),
            Commands = make_set(ActingProcessCommandLine),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
         by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessId, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc

[LLM] Fake pgsql-monitor.service systemd persistence written under ~/.config/systemd/user/ Installation High
Detects creation of the article-named `pgsql-monitor.service` user-level systemd unit file, and the follow-up `systemctl --user daemon-reload` spawned by a python3 process — the exact persistence mechanism each of the four managed.pyz collector instances installs. Rationale: Article names the exact persistence artefact (`pgsql-monitor.service`) and the exact cmdline (`systemctl --user daemon-reload`) spawned by each of the four parallel managed.pyz instances. User-level systemd persistence under `~/.config/systemd/user/` is rare on CI runners and cloud-workload base images. No external sources cross-checked.
ATT&CKT1543.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes

  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where (FolderPath has "/.config/systemd/user" and FileName endswith ".service")

  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Signal="FileWrite";
let daemon_reload = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "systemctl"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "--user" and ProcessCommandLine has "daemon-reload"
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName="systemctl", FolderPath=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Signal="DaemonReload";
union file_persist, daemon_reload
| order by Timestamp desc

     or TargetFileName =~ "pgsql-monitor.service"

  | where ParentProcessName in~ ("python","python3")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath=ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName="systemctl", ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine=ParentProcessCommandLine, Signal="DaemonReload";
union file_persist, daemon_reload

[LLM] Burst of AWS SSM SendCommand / StartSession from stolen durabletask credentials Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the article's lateral-movement pattern: stolen ~/.aws/credentials being used to enumerate SSM-managed instances and run remote commands or shell sessions. Looks for a single IAM principal calling DescribeInstanceInformation followed by SendCommand or StartSession from a fresh source IP within a short window. Rationale: Article confirms `propagates to other machines through AWS SSM and Kubernetes kubectl exec` after harvesting AWS credentials from ~/.aws/credentials. The high-signal pattern is DescribeInstanceInformation immediately followed by SendCommand or StartSession from the same principal within a short window — classic SSM-as-RCE TTP. Hunting tier because legitimate ops engineers do this too. Defender / Sentinel KQL left empty because their canonical schemas in this tenant do not include AWSCloudTrail; the Sentinel column list above contains no AWSCloudTrail table — operators ingesting CloudTrail via the AWS S3 connector would have a `AWSCloudTrail` table not in the canonical schema. No external sources cross-checked.
ATT&CKT1021.007 T1078.004 T1580
Data sourcesAuthentication
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:(DescribeInstanceInformation OR SendCommand OR StartSession OR ResumeSession) @evt.outcome:success @userIdentity.type:(IAMUser OR AssumedRole)
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, sourceIPAddress, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.userName, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName, awsRegion, requestParameters.instanceIds, requestParameters.documentName, requestParameters.target
| filter eventSource = "ssm.amazonaws.com"
      and eventName in ["DescribeInstanceInformation", "SendCommand", "StartSession", "ResumeSession", "GetCommandInvocation"]
      and not isPresent(errorCode)
| stats count(*) as calls, count_distinct(eventName) as event_types, count_distinct(sourceIPAddress) as src_ips, earliest(@timestamp) as first_seen, latest(@timestamp) as last_seen by userIdentity.arn
| filter event_types >= 2
| sort last_seen desc
CLOUD
`cloudtrail` (eventName=DescribeInstanceInformation OR eventName=SendCommand OR eventName=StartSession OR eventName=ResumeSession) errorCode="*" OR errorCode=NULL
| eval principal=coalesce('userIdentity.arn','userIdentity.userName')
| stats earliest(_time) as firstSeen latest(_time) as lastSeen dc(eventName) as eventTypes values(eventName) as events values(sourceIPAddress) as srcIPs dc(sourceIPAddress) as srcIPCount count by principal
| where eventTypes >= 2 AND srcIPCount >= 1
| eval windowSec=lastSeen-firstSeen
| where windowSec <= 1800
| convert ctime(firstSeen) ctime(lastSeen)
| sort - firstSeen

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc") or SHA1 in~ ("069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc") or MD5 in~ ("069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc") or SHA1 in~ ("069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc") or MD5 in~ ("069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Free Apps Are Quietly Turning Smart TVs Into Web-Scraping Proxies for AI

The Hacker News
2026-06-06 9 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A researcher has reverse-engineered the iOS SDK that Bright Data embeds in consumer apps and documented how it turns devices, including always-on smart TVs, into exit nodes that relay web-scraping traffic for a data business Bright Data markets heavily to the AI industry. The company, the successor to Luminati, operates what it calls the largest residential proxy network in the world,

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Bright Data partner-app or brdsdk.framework present on managed iOS / mobile inventory
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Bright Data SDK control-plane beacon to proxyjs/clientsdk endpoints · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Smart-TV / mobile device acting as residential proxy exit node (high-fan-out HTTPS to unrelated public destinations) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] Bright Data SDK control-plane beacon to proxyjs/clientsdk endpoints Command & Control High
Detects DNS or TLS SNI resolution to the Bright Data residential-proxy SDK control channels (proxyjs/clientsdk on bright-sdk.com, brdtnet.com, luminatinet.com). Any endpoint resolving these is either running an app embedding brdsdk.framework or actively relaying scraping jobs as an exit node. Rationale: All five FQDNs (proxyjs.brdtnet.com, proxyjs.luminatinet.com, proxyjs.bright-sdk.com, clientsdk.bright-sdk.com, clientsdk.brdtnet.com) are explicitly named in the article body and corroborated by the Include Security research blog as the SDK's exclusive control-plane channel — the article itself recommends blocking them at the router. The article also notes Bright Data's paid commercial service runs on different hosts, so hits here are specifically the embedded-SDK exit-node behaviour. Cross-checked against the Include Security research blog (https://blog.includesecurity.com/2026/06/the-smart-tv-in-your-livingroom-is-a-node-in-the-aiscraping-economy/) which added the broader *.luminati.io SNI pattern and the brdsdk.framework binary identifier. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.includesecurity.com/2026/06/the-smart-tv-in-your-livingroom-is-a-node-in-the-aiscraping-economy/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
// Bright Data residential-proxy SDK control-plane beacon
// Endpoints contacting *.bright-sdk.com / *.brdtnet.com / *.luminatinet.com
let brdControlHosts = dynamic(["proxyjs.brdtnet.com","proxyjs.luminatinet.com","proxyjs.bright-sdk.com","clientsdk.bright-sdk.com","clientsdk.brdtnet.com"]);
let brdSuffixes = dynamic([".bright-sdk.com",".brdtnet.com",".luminatinet.com",".luminati.io"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl in~ (brdControlHosts)
    or RemoteUrl has_any (brdSuffixes)
| extend MatchType = case(RemoteUrl in~ (brdControlHosts), "control-plane FQDN",
                          RemoteUrl endswith ".bright-sdk.com", "bright-sdk.com suffix",
                          RemoteUrl endswith ".brdtnet.com", "brdtnet.com suffix",
                          RemoteUrl endswith ".luminatinet.com", "luminatinet.com suffix",
                          RemoteUrl endswith ".luminati.io", "luminati.io suffix",
                          "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, MatchType
| order by Timestamp desc
// Bright Data residential-proxy SDK control-plane beacon — ASIM DNS view
let brdControlHosts = dynamic(["proxyjs.brdtnet.com","proxyjs.luminatinet.com","proxyjs.bright-sdk.com","clientsdk.bright-sdk.com","clientsdk.brdtnet.com"]);
let brdSuffixes = dynamic([".bright-sdk.com",".brdtnet.com",".luminatinet.com",".luminati.io"]);
(union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where DnsQuery in~ (brdControlHosts)
       or DnsQuery has_any (brdSuffixes)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Indicator = DnsQuery, Source = "ImDnsActivity"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where isnotempty(DestinationHostName)
   | where DestinationHostName in~ (brdControlHosts)
       or DestinationHostName has_any (brdSuffixes)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr = SourceIP, SrcHostname = SourceHostName, SrcUsername = SourceUserName,
             Indicator = DestinationHostName, Source = strcat(DeviceVendor,"/",DeviceProduct)),
  (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where Name has_any (brdSuffixes) or Name in~ (brdControlHosts)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr = ClientIP, SrcHostname = Computer, SrcUsername = "", Indicator = Name, Source = "DnsEvents"))
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count(),
            Indicators = make_set(Indicator, 25), Sources = make_set(Source, 5)
            by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname
| order by LastSeen desc

[LLM] Bright Data partner-app or brdsdk.framework present on managed iOS / mobile inventory Installation Medium
Hunts the managed mobile/endpoint fleet for installed apps that ship the Bright Data residential-proxy SDK (brdsdk.framework v1.532.120) — using the article-named partner-app list (Petflix, PlayWorks Digital, CloudTV, Longvision) and Bright Data's published partner page. Catches the exit-node *at install time* rather than waiting for it to phone home. Rationale: Article explicitly names Petflix (Roku), PlayWorks Digital, CloudTV, and Longvision as Bright Data partners shipping the SDK, and identifies brdsdk.framework v1.532.120 as the binary. Include Security additionally surfaced the Swift symbols BrdWebSocketFacade and BrdNetwork.DNSResolver inside the framework. Article notes the partner list is not 1:1 with current SDK inclusion (each app must be verified independently), so this is a hunt not an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.includesecurity.com/2026/06/the-smart-tv-in-your-livingroom-is-a-node-in-the-aiscraping-economy/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1474.003

[LLM] Smart-TV / mobile device acting as residential proxy exit node (high-fan-out HTTPS to unrelated public destinations) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts firewall and NetFlow telemetry for the behavioural signature of a Bright Data exit node: a single internal source (typically an unmanaged smart TV or mobile device) initiates a high volume of outbound HTTPS sessions to many unrelated public web destinations the user is not actively browsing, often during off-hours. The 200 GB/month SDK cap and the device's always-on TV / mobile profile shape the threshold. Rationale: Article quantifies the SDK's monthly traffic ceiling (200 GB/mo, uncapped in some regions) and notes the device 'keeps relaying in the background while someone is watching the screen or on a call, as long as the battery is not low'. The behavioural fingerprint — single internal source, hundreds of unrelated public destinations per hour, outbound bytes ≈ inbound bytes (proxy relay, not browsing) — is what survives even if Bright Data rotates control-plane domains. Article warns 'Bright Data could also change how the SDK connects in the future, which would mean any blocklist needs updating' which is exactly why a behavioural UC complements UC1's IOC UC. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.includesecurity.com/2026/06/the-smart-tv-in-your-livingroom-is-a-node-in-the-aiscraping-economy/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1496 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
// Managed iOS / mobile exhibiting residential-proxy egress pattern (covers Defender for iOS estate)
let WindowHrs = 1h;
let MinUniqueRemoteIPs = 100;   // residential browsing rarely fans out to >100 distinct public IPs per hour
let MinSessions = 500;          // SDK polling + scraping job throughput floor
let ManagedMobile = DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(24h)
    | where OSPlatform in ("iOS","iPadOS","Android")
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, DeviceType, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers) by DeviceId, DeviceName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| join kind=inner ManagedMobile on DeviceId
| summarize UniqueRemoteIPs = dcount(RemoteIP),
            UniqueRemoteUrls = dcount(RemoteUrl),
            Sessions = count(),
            SampleUrls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 25),
            SampleProcess = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, bin(Timestamp, WindowHrs)
| where UniqueRemoteIPs > MinUniqueRemoteIPs and Sessions > MinSessions
| extend MultiUseSig = iff(UniqueRemoteUrls > 200 and array_length(SampleProcess) <= 2, "likely-proxy", "review")
| order by Sessions desc
// Residential-proxy exit-node behavioural hunt against firewall logs
// Surfaces internal sources fan-out HTTPS to many unrelated public destinations (Bright Data exit-node signature)
let WindowHrs = 1h;
let MinUniqueDests = 250;       // home/IoT devices very rarely exceed this per hour
let MinBytesOut = 524288000;    // 500 MB outbound per hour (200 GB/mo SDK cap → ~280 MB/hr avg, peaks higher)
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DeviceVendor in ("Palo Alto Networks","Fortinet","Cisco","Check Point","Zscaler","SonicWall")
| where DestinationPort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and isnotempty(DestinationIP)
| where ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP) == false
| summarize UniqueDestHosts = dcount(DestinationHostName),
            UniqueDestIPs = dcount(DestinationIP),
            BytesOut = sum(toint(SentBytes)),
            BytesIn = sum(toint(ReceivedBytes)),
            Sessions = count(),
            SampleHosts = make_set(DestinationHostName, 25)
            by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowHrs)
| where UniqueDestHosts > MinUniqueDests and BytesOut > MinBytesOut
| extend GbOut = round(BytesOut / 1073741824.0, 2)
| extend EgressInboundRatio = round(BytesOut * 1.0 / (BytesIn + 1), 2)
| where EgressInboundRatio > 0.4   // proxy traffic: outbound ~= inbound, unlike normal browsing which is inbound-heavy
| order by BytesOut desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count

| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

[LLM] SolarWinds Serv-U pre-auth DoS exploit (CVE-2026-28318) — POST with Content-Encoding: deflate Exploitation High
Detects the specific exploit pattern for CVE-2026-28318: an unauthenticated POST request to a SolarWinds Serv-U file server that carries a Content-Encoding: deflate header, which crashes the Serv-U service. SolarWinds itself recommends blocking any request containing a content-encoding header because the vulnerable service doesn't legitimately use it, making the header presence a high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Article and SolarWinds advisory explicitly call out the trigger: an unauthenticated POST with a Content-Encoding: deflate header crashing Serv-U. The vendor's mitigation guidance — block any request containing a content-encoding header because the vulnerable service doesn't use it — turns header presence into a near-zero-FP signal. Defender query pivots on Serv-U.exe process restarts paired with bursty inbound connections since Defender XDR doesn't natively capture HTTP request headers. Cross-checked against CISA KEV catalog entry and SolarWinds Trust Center advisory wording quoted in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://www.solarwinds.com/trust-center/security-advisories • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-28318

| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            arg_max(Timestamp, *)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where ConnCount > 50
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "Serv-U.exe" or FileName =~ "RhinoSoft.Serv-U.exe"
    | where ActionType in ("ProcessCreated","ProcessTerminated")
) on DeviceName
| where ProcessCreationTime between (Timestamp - 10m .. Timestamp + 10m)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ConnCount, ProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCreationTime
| order by Timestamp desc
// Detect POST requests to Serv-U carrying Content-Encoding header — CVE-2026-28318 pre-auth DoS
// Vendor advisory: header is never legitimately used by Serv-U, so any presence is high-fidelity
let ServUHosts = dynamic(["servu","serv-u","sftp","ftp"]);
let ServUPorts = dynamic([21, 22, 80, 443, 990, 8080, 8443]);
(union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
   | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
   | where DestinationPort in (ServUPorts)
   | where Message has "content-encoding" or Message has "Content-Encoding"
            or RequestContext has "content-encoding" or RequestContext has "Content-Encoding"
            or RequestClientApplication has "deflate"
            or DeviceCustomString1 has "content-encoding" or DeviceCustomString2 has "content-encoding"
            or DeviceCustomString3 has "content-encoding" or DeviceCustomString4 has "content-encoding"
            or DeviceCustomString5 has "content-encoding" or DeviceCustomString6 has "content-encoding"
   | extend Host = tolower(DestinationHostName)
   | where Host has_any (ServUHosts) or DestinationServiceName has_any (ServUHosts) or isempty(Host)
   | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort,
             RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct),
  (W3CIISLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
   | where csMethod =~ "POST"
   | where sSiteName has_any (ServUHosts) or Computer has_any (ServUHosts)
   | project TimeGenerated, cIP, Computer, sSiteName, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, scSubStatus, csUserAgent),
  (Syslog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
   | where ProcessName has_any ("Serv-U","serv-u","servu")
   | where SyslogMessage has "content-encoding" or SyslogMessage has "deflate" or SyslogMessage has "crash" or SyslogMessage has "terminated"
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage))
| order by TimeGenerated desc
